# ggplot {#sec-ggplot} ## Learning objectives By the end of this chapter, you will be able to: - Understand the basic structure of a ggplot and how it builds layer by layer. - Map data variables to visual aesthetics like position, colour and shape. - Add and customise plot elements such as labels, themes, and titles. - Use facets to compare subgroups effectively. - Apply best practices for clear, meaningful visualisations. Data visualisation helps us see relationships, patterns and surprises that tables of numbers can easily hide. In this chapter, we’ll use **ggplot2** [@R-ggplot2], part of the tidyverse, to build clear graphics step by step. We’ll use our dataset of penguin measurements to explore how penguin species differ in body size and bill (culmen) dimensions. You’ll learn how to go from a simple scatterplot to polished figures. :::{.callout-note} This appendix is pre-course material: an introduction to building plots with ggplot2. Day 3 (Blocks 1–5) builds on it and covers figure design, themes, scales, extensions and saving in more depth. The `penguins` data used here is loaded from `files/chapter5.RDS` (download it below and read it in with `readRDS()`). It keeps the original column names from the raw Palmer data, so bill measurements are called `culmen_length_mm` and `culmen_depth_mm`. In `palmerpenguins::penguins` and in the Day 3 chapters the same columns are called `bill_length_mm` and `bill_depth_mm`. ::: :::{.callout-tip} If you are struggling to write the code for your ggplot, try loading the `esquisse` @R-esquisse add-in to produce a point-and-click interface that will help you build your plot and produce R code at the end. ::: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: ## Building plots We’ll be using the `ggplot2` package to create data visualisations. It’s part of the `tidyverse` suite of packages. Although many people refer to it simply as `ggplot`, its official name is `ggplot2`. ::: grid ::: g-col-6 **ggplot2** uses a layered grammar of graphics, where plots are constructed through a series of layers. You start with a base layer (by calling `ggplot`), then add **data** and **aesthetics**, followed by selecting the appropriate **geometries** for the plot. These first 3 layers give you the simplest version of a complete plot. You can then make the plot clearer and better looking by adding further layers such as **scales**, **facets**, **coordinates**, **labels** and **themes**. ::: ::: g-col-6 ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](images/gglayers.png){fig-align='center' width=80%} ::: ::: ::: ::: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} head(penguins) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|study_name | sample_number|species |region |island |stage |individual_id |clutch_completion |date_egg | culmen_length_mm| culmen_depth_mm| flipper_length_mm| body_mass_g|sex | delta_15_n_o_oo| delta_13_c_o_oo|comments | year|mass_range | |:----------|-------------:|:-------|:------|:---------|:------------------|:-------------|:-----------------|:----------|----------------:|---------------:|-----------------:|-----------:|:------|---------------:|---------------:|:------------------------------|----:|:------------| |PAL0708 | 1|Adelie |Anvers |Torgersen |Adult, 1 Egg Stage |N1A1 |Yes |2007-11-11 | 39.1| 18.7| 181| 3750|Male | NA| NA|Not enough blood for isotopes. | 2007|mid penguin | |PAL0708 | 2|Adelie |Anvers |Torgersen |Adult, 1 Egg Stage |N1A2 |Yes |2007-11-11 | 39.5| 17.4| 186| 3800|Female | 8.94956| -24.69454|NA | 2007|mid penguin | |PAL0708 | 3|Adelie |Anvers |Torgersen |Adult, 1 Egg Stage |N2A1 |Yes |2007-11-16 | 40.3| 18.0| 195| 3250|Female | 8.36821| -25.33302|NA | 2007|smol penguin | |PAL0708 | 4|Adelie |Anvers |Torgersen |Adult, 1 Egg Stage |N2A2 |Yes |2007-11-16 | NA| NA| NA| NA|NA | NA| NA|Adult not sampled. | 2007|NA | |PAL0708 | 5|Adelie |Anvers |Torgersen |Adult, 1 Egg Stage |N3A1 |Yes |2007-11-16 | 36.7| 19.3| 193| 3450|Female | 8.76651| -25.32426|NA | 2007|smol penguin | |PAL0708 | 6|Adelie |Anvers |Torgersen |Adult, 1 Egg Stage |N3A2 |Yes |2007-11-16 | 39.3| 20.6| 190| 3650|Male | 8.66496| -25.29805|NA | 2007|mid penguin |
::: ::: Let’s build a basic scatterplot to show the relationship between `flipper_length_mm` and `body_mass_g`. We will customise the plots further in later sections; for now, this gives a quick overview of the different layers. * **Layer 1** creates the base plot that we build upon. * **Layer 2** adds the `data` and some `aesthetics`: * The data is passed as the first argument. * Aesthetics are added via the mapping argument, where you define your variables (e.g., x or both x and y). This also lets you specify general properties, like the colour for grouping variables. * **Layer 3** adds geometries, or `geom_?` for short. This tells ggplot how to display the data points. Remember to add these layers with a `+`, rather than using a pipe (`|>` or `%>%`). You can also add multiple geoms if needed, for example, combining a violin plot with a boxplot. * **Layer 4** includes `scale_?` functions, which let you customise aesthetics like colour. You can do much more with scales, but we'll explore that later. * **Layer 5** introduces facets, such as `facet_wrap()`, allowing you to add an extra dimension to your plot by showing the relationship you are interested in for each level of a categorical variable. * **Layer 6** involves coordinates, where `coord_cartesian()` controls the limits for the x- and y-axes (xlim and ylim), enabling you to zoom in or out of the plot. * **Layer 7** helps you modify axis labels. * **Layer 8** controls the overall style of the plot, including background colour, text size and borders. R provides several predefined themes, such as `theme_classic`, `theme_bw`, `theme_minimal`, and `theme_light`. Click on the tabs below to see how each layer contributes to refining the plot. ::: {.panel-tabset} ## Layer 1 ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](12a-ggplot_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-5-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: There’s not much to see at this stage - this is basically an empty plot layer. ## Layer 2 ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(data = penguins, mapping = aes(x = body_mass_g, y = flipper_length_mm)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](12a-ggplot_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-6-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: You won’t see any data points yet because we haven’t specified how to display them. However, we have mapped the aesthetics, indicating that we want to plot `body_mass_g` on the x-axis and `flipper_length_mm` on the y-axis. This also sets the axis titles, as well as the axis values and breakpoints. ::: callout-tip You don’t need to include `data =` or `mapping =` if you keep those arguments in the default order. Similarly, the first column name you enter in the `aes()` function will automatically be interpreted as the x variable, and the second as y, so you can omit specifying `x` and `y` if you prefer. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(penguins, aes(body_mass_g, flipper_length_mm)) ``` ::: will give you the same output as the code above. ::: ## Layer 3 ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(data = penguins, mapping = aes(x = body_mass_g, y = flipper_length_mm, colour = sex)) + geom_point() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](12a-ggplot_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-8-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: Here we are telling `ggplot` to add a scatterplot. You may notice a warning indicating that some rows were removed due to missing values. The `colour` argument adds colour to the points based on a grouping variable (in this case, `sex`). If you want all the points to be black (showing only two dimensions rather than three), omit the `colour` argument. ## Layer 4 ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(data = penguins, mapping = aes(x = body_mass_g, y = flipper_length_mm, colour = sex)) + geom_point() + # changes colour palette scale_colour_brewer(palette = "Dark2") + # add breaks from 2500 to 6500 in increasing steps of 500 scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(from = 2500, to = 6500, by = 500)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](12a-ggplot_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-9-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: The `scale_?` functions allow us to modify the colour palette of the plot, adjust axis breaks, and more. You could change the axis labels within `scale_x_continuous()` as well or leave it for Layer 7. ## Layer 5 ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(data = penguins, mapping = aes(x=body_mass_g, y=flipper_length_mm, colour=sex)) + geom_point() + scale_colour_brewer(palette = "Dark2") + # split main plot up into different subplots by species facet_wrap(~ species) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](12a-ggplot_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-10-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: In this step, we’re using faceting to split the plot by species. ## Layer 6 ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(data = penguins, mapping = aes(x=body_mass_g, y=flipper_length_mm, colour=sex)) + geom_point() + scale_colour_brewer(palette = "Dark2") + facet_wrap(~ species) + # limits the range of the y axis coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 250)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](12a-ggplot_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-11-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: Here we adjust the limits of the y-axis to zoom out of the plot. If you want to zoom in or out of the x-axis, you can add the `xlim` argument to the `coord_cartesian()` function. ## Layer 7 ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(data = penguins, mapping = aes(x=body_mass_g, y=flipper_length_mm, colour=sex)) + geom_point() + scale_colour_brewer(palette = "Dark2") + facet_wrap(~ species) + labs(x = "Body Mass (in g)", # labels the x axis y = "Flipper length (in mm)", # labels the y axis colour = "Sex") # labels the grouping variable in the legend ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](12a-ggplot_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-12-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: You can change the axis labels using the `labs()` function, or you can modify them when adjusting the scales (e.g., within the `scale_x_continuous()` function). ## Layer 8 ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(data = penguins, mapping = aes(x=body_mass_g, y=flipper_length_mm, colour=sex)) + geom_point() + scale_colour_brewer(palette = "Dark2") + facet_wrap(~ species) + labs(x = "Body Mass (in g)", y = "Flipper length (in mm)", colour = "Sex") + # add a theme theme_classic() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](12a-ggplot_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-13-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: The `theme_classic()` function is applied to change the overall appearance of the plot. ::: ::: callout-important You need the first three layers to create your base plot. Everything else is optional, so you don’t need to use all eight layers. Layers 4-8 can be added in any order (more or less), whereas layers 1-3 must follow a fixed sequence. ::: ## Exploring common geom types So far we have only made a scatterplot, but ggplot offers many more geoms. This chapter works through some of the most common ones. | Data type | Example geom | Purpose | |------------------------|-----------------------------------------------|----------------------| | Continuous–continuous | `geom_point()`, `geom_line()`, `geom_smooth()` | Relationships/trends | | Categorical–continuous | `geom_boxplot()`, `geom_violin()`, `geom_col()` | Comparisons | | Continuous | `geom_histogram()`, `geom_density()` | Distributions | ## Histogram (`geom_histogram()`) {#sec-hist} If you want to show the **distribution of a continuous variable**, you can use a histogram. As with every plot, you need at least 3 layers to create a base version of the plot. `geom_histogram()` only needs an `x` variable, because it does the counting "in the background". A histogram divides the data into "bins" (i.e., groupings displayed in a single bar). These bins are plotted along the x-axis, with the y-axis showing the count of observations in each bin. It's basically a barchart for continuous variables. Let's have a look at the weight distribution in our dataset. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(penguins, aes(x = body_mass_g)) + geom_histogram() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Default histogram](12a-ggplot_files/figure-html/fig-hist-1.png){#fig-hist fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: The default **number of bins** is 30 (as shown in @fig-hist above). Changing the number of bins (argument `bins`) makes the histogram coarser or finer. More bins show more detail. Perhaps it’s more intuitive to modify the **width of each bin** using the `binwidth` argument. For example, `binwidth = 1` for the weight category would mean each "weight group" represents 1 g, while `binwidth = 50` would group weights into 50 g spans. The plots below show modifications for both `bins` and `binwidth`. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} #less finetuning ggplot(penguins, aes(x = body_mass_g)) + geom_histogram(bins = 10) # more fineturning ggplot(penguins, aes(x = body_mass_g)) + geom_histogram(binwidth = 50) ``` ::: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Bins vs binwidth arguments](12a-ggplot_files/figure-html/fig-bins-1.png){#fig-bins fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: The **warning message** tells us 2 rows of data were removed due to containing `non-finite outside the scale range`. Have a look at the body mass column (penguins) to see if you can decipher the warning message. The rows were removed because . Click through each tab to see how you can modify colours, axis labels, margins, and breaks, and apply a different theme. ::: {.panel-tabset} ## Colour We can change the plot colours by adding a **fill argument** and a **colour argument**. The `fill` argument changes the colour of the bars, while the `colour` argument modifies the outline of the bars. Note that these arguments are **added directly to the `geom_histogram()`**, rather than within the overall `aes()`, because we want every bar to be the same colour rather than mapping colour to a variable. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(penguins, aes(x = body_mass_g)) + geom_histogram(binwidth = 50, fill = "#586cfd", colour = "#FC58BE") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](12a-ggplot_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-15-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: ::: callout-tip You could use: * Hex codes for `fill` and `colour`, as we did here: `geom_histogram(binwidth = 50, fill = "#586cfd", colour = "#FC58BE")`. If you want to create your own colours, check out [this website](https://www.hexcolortool.com/){target="_blank"}. * Pre-defined colour names: `geom_histogram(binwidth = 50, fill = "purple", colour = "green")`. See the full list [here](https://www.datanovia.com/en/blog/awesome-list-of-657-r-color-names/){target="_blank"}. ::: ## Axes labels, margins, and breaks Here we **removed the label** for the y-axis `Count` (to show you some variety) and **modified the breaks**. The y-axis is now displayed in increasing steps of 5, and the x-axis has a break every 500 g. Notice how the `breaks =` argument changes the labels of the break ticks but not the scale limits. You can adjust the limits of the scale using the `limits =` argument. To make the effect obvious, we set the limits to 2000 and 7000. See how the values from 2000 to 2500, and 6500 to 7000 do not have labels? You would need to adjust that using the `breaks =` argument. The `expansion()` function removes the gap between the x-axis and the bars. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(penguins, aes(x = body_mass_g)) + geom_histogram(binwidth = 50, fill = "#586cfd", colour = "#FC58BE") + labs(x = "Body mass in (g)", # renaming x axis label y = "") + # removing the y axis label scale_y_continuous( # remove the space below the bars (first number), but keep a tiny bit (5%) above (second number) expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.05)), # changing break points on y axis breaks = seq(from = 0, to = 20, by = 5) ) + scale_x_continuous( # changing break points on x axis breaks = seq(from = 2500, to = 6500, by = 500), # Experimenting with the scale limits limits = c(2000, 7000) ) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](12a-ggplot_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-16-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: ## Themes Let's experiment with the themes. For this plot we have chosen `theme_bw()`: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(penguins, aes(x = body_mass_g)) + geom_histogram(binwidth = 50, fill = "#586cfd", colour = "#FC58BE") + labs(x = "Body mass in (g)", # renaming x axis label y = "") + # removing the y axis label scale_y_continuous( # remove the space below the bars (first number), but keep a tiny bit (5%) above (second number) expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.05)), # changing break points on y axis breaks = seq(from = 0, to = 20, by = 5) ) + scale_x_continuous( # changing break points on x axis breaks = seq(from = 2500, to = 6500, by = 500), # Experimenting with the scale limits limits = c(2000, 7000) )+ theme_bw() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](12a-ggplot_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-17-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: ::: ## Scatterplot (`geom_point()`) {#sec-scatter} Scatterplots are appropriate when you want to plot **two continuous variables**. We can also **add a trendline** by using `geom_smooth()`. The default trendline is `loess`. If you want a linear trendline, you would need to add `method = "lm"` inside the `geom_smooth()` function. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(data = penguins, aes(x=culmen_length_mm, y=culmen_depth_mm)) + geom_point() + geom_smooth() ggplot(data = penguins, aes(x=culmen_length_mm, y=culmen_depth_mm)) + geom_point() + geom_smooth(method = lm) ``` ::: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Default Scatterplot with added trendline - loess (left) and linear (right)](12a-ggplot_files/figure-html/fig-scatter-1.png){#fig-scatter fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: Customising the colour of a scatterplot is slightly different from the other plots we’ve encountered so far. Technically, the point is not a "filled-in black area" but rather an extremely wide outline of a circle. Therefore, we cannot use the usual `fill` argument and instead need to use the `colour` argument, similar to how we customised the outline of the histogram. See the tabs below to learn how to change the colour for all points or how to adjust the colour based on groupings. ::: {.panel-tabset} ## Colour for all points If we want to **change the colour of all the points**, we can add the `colour` argument to the `geom_point()` function. Likewise, to change the **colour of the trendline**, we would also use the `colour` argument. Here, we used pre-defined colour names, but HEX codes would work just as well. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} # colour of all points and the trendline ggplot(data = penguins, aes(x=culmen_length_mm, y=culmen_depth_mm)) + geom_point(colour = "darkorange")+ geom_smooth(method = "lm", colour = "darkblue") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](12a-ggplot_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-19-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: ## Colour with grouping If we want the points to **change colour based on another grouping variable**, the `colour` argument should go inside the `aes()`. If you don’t want to define the colours manually, you can use a colour palette like Brewer (`scale_colour_brewer()`) or Viridis (`scale_colour_viridis_d()`). ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} ## adding grouping variable species and changing the colour values manually ggplot(data = penguins, aes(x=culmen_length_mm, y=culmen_depth_mm, colour = species)) + geom_point()+ geom_smooth(method = "lm")+ scale_colour_manual(values = c("darkorange", "cyan", "purple")) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](12a-ggplot_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-20-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: ::: {.callout-important collapse="true" icon="false"} ## What happened to the direction of correlation? Colouring the points by species reveals a reversal of the apparent correlation. This is known as Simpson's Paradox, and is a result of "Omitted Variable Bias": our original scatterplot did not include the confounder, species. Omitting important variables can lead to incorrect conclusions. ::: ## Legend title and labels You can tidy the legend title and group labels using the `scale_colour_?` function, depending on the palette you’re using (e.g., `scale_colour_manual()`, `scale_colour_brewer` and many more). ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(data = penguins, aes(x=culmen_length_mm, y=culmen_depth_mm, colour = species)) + geom_point()+ geom_smooth(method = "lm")+ scale_colour_manual(values = c("darkorange", "cyan", "purple"), name = "Species", labels = c("Adelie penguin", "Chinstrap penguin", "Gentoo penguin")) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](12a-ggplot_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-21-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: ::: :::{.task} ::::{.task-header} Your turn :::: ::::{.task-container} All other layers remain exactly the same as in other plots. Try adding layers to make the plot above prettier: * [ ] 1. relabel axes x and y * [ ] 2. move the legend to a different position (either top, left, or bottom) * [ ] 3. add a theme ::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"} ## More hints If you are experiencing issues with the legend position and theme, try modifying the order of the layers. :::
::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(data = penguins, aes(x=culmen_length_mm, y=culmen_depth_mm, colour = species)) + geom_point()+ geom_smooth(method = "lm", show.legend = FALSE)+ # stop this layer from appearing in the legend. scale_colour_manual(values = c("darkorange", "cyan", "purple"), name = "Species", labels = c("Adelie penguin", "Chinstrap penguin", "Gentoo penguin"))+ labs(x = "Bill length (mm)", y = "Bill depth (mm)")+ theme_classic() + # place before moving the legend position theme(legend.position = "top") # move legend to the top ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](12a-ggplot_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-22-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: :::
:::: ::: ## Boxplot (`geom_boxplot()`) A boxplot is one way to display a **continuous variable with a categorical grouping variable**. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} # default boxplot ggplot(penguins, aes(x = species, y = body_mass_g))+ geom_boxplot() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](12a-ggplot_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-23-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: Tada! As usual, we can enhance the plot by adding various layers. Click on each tab below to see how. ::: {.panel-tabset} ## Colour We can change the colour by adding a `fill` argument inside the `aes()`. To customise the colours further, we can add a `scale_fill_?` layer. If you have specific colours in mind, use `scale_fill_manual()`. If you prefer pre-defined palettes, such as Brewer, you can use `scale_fill_brewer()`. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(penguins, aes(x = species, y = body_mass_g, fill = species))+ geom_boxplot()+ # customise colour scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Dark2") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](12a-ggplot_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-24-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: ## Axes labels We need to relabel the axes. The function to use depends on the variable type. Here, we need `scale_x_discrete()` for the x-axis and `scale_y_continuous()` for the y-axis. We can also tidy up the group labels and adjust the breaks on the y-axis (e.g., in steps of 500 g) within these same functions. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(penguins, aes(x = species, y = body_mass_g, fill = species))+ geom_boxplot()+ scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Dark2")+ scale_x_discrete( # changing the label of x name = "Species", # changing the group labels of the 3 groups labels = c("Adelie penguin", "Chinstrap penguin", "Gentoo penguin")) + scale_y_continuous( # changing name of the y axis name = "Body mass (g)", # changing break labels breaks = c(seq(from = 3000, to = 6000, by = 500)) ) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](12a-ggplot_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-25-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: ## Legend and theme The legend is superfluous; best to take it off. We can remove the legend by adding the argument `guide = "none"` to the `scale_fill_?` function. Let's pick a theme we haven't used yet: `theme_dark()`. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(penguins, aes(x = species, y = body_mass_g, fill = species))+ geom_boxplot()+ scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Dark2", guide = "none")+ scale_x_discrete( # changing the label of x name = "Species", # changing the group labels of the 3 groups labels = c("Adelie penguin", "Chinstrap penguin", "Gentoo penguin")) + scale_y_continuous( # changing name of the y axis name = "Body mass (g)", # changing break labels breaks = c(seq(from = 3000, to = 6000, by = 500)) ) + theme_dark() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](12a-ggplot_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-26-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: ::: ## Violin plot (`geom_violin()`) An alternative way to display a **continuous variable with a categorical grouping variable** is a violin plot. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} # default violin plot ggplot(penguins, aes(x = species, y = body_mass_g, fill = species))+ geom_violin() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](12a-ggplot_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-27-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: :::{.task} ::::{.task-header} Your turn :::: ::::{.task-container} Adjusting the violin plot would be exactly the same as the boxplot. Try to add layers to the base plot above to: * [ ] change the colours either manually or using a pre-defined colour palette * [ ] tidy the axes labels and group names * [ ] in case a legend appears, take it off * [ ] add a theme
::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(penguins, aes(x = species, y = body_mass_g, fill = species))+ geom_violin()+ scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Dark2", guide = "none")+ scale_x_discrete( # changing the label of x name = "Species", # changing the group labels of the 3 groups labels = c("Adelie penguin", "Chinstrap penguin", "Gentoo penguin")) + scale_y_continuous( # changing name of the y axis name = "Body mass (g)", # changing break labels breaks = c(seq(from = 3000, to = 6000, by = 500)) )+ theme_bw() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](12a-ggplot_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-28-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: :::
:::: ::: ## Violin-boxplots So far, we’ve only added one `geom_?` layer to our plots. However, thanks to ggplot's layered system, we can add multiple geoms, for example, when creating a violin-boxplot. Remember, the order of the layers can sometimes make a difference. We've seen this already - adding a theme at the end can override earlier arguments like the legend position. Similarly, `ggplot + violinplot + boxplot` will look different from `ggplot + boxplot + violinplot`. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(penguins, aes(x = species, y = body_mass_g, fill = species))+ geom_violin()+ geom_boxplot() ggplot(penguins, aes(x = species, y = body_mass_g, fill = species))+ geom_boxplot() + geom_violin() ``` ::: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Default violin-boxplot: Order of the layer matters](12a-ggplot_files/figure-html/fig-vb_bv-1.png){#fig-vb_bv fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: See the tabs below to learn how to customise various elements, such as the width of the boxes, and the colour or opacity. ::: {.panel-tabset} ## Width of the boxes If we want to get any information from the boxplot, we need to place it "on top of" the violin plot. But still, the boxplot is pretty wide and covers important details from the violin plot. To make the information more visible, we can **adjust the width of the boxes**. Finding an appropriate width might take some trial and error. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(penguins, aes(x = species, y = body_mass_g, fill = species))+ geom_violin()+ geom_boxplot(width = .2) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Default violin-boxplot: adjusting width of the box](12a-ggplot_files/figure-html/fig-vb_width-1.png){#fig-vb_width fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: ## Colour Adding colour should be pretty straightforward by now. The code is no different from what we used for the boxplot or violin plot. We need to add the `fill` argument within the `aes()`, along with a `scale_fill_?` layer. However, we can further customise the plot by adding an **opacity argument** using `alpha` to the violin plot geom. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(penguins, aes(x = species, y = body_mass_g, fill = species))+ geom_violin(alpha = 0.4) + # alpha for opacity geom_boxplot(width = 0.2) + # change width of the boxes scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Dark2") # customise colour ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Violin-boxplot with a different colour palette](12a-ggplot_files/figure-html/fig-vb_colour-1.png){#fig-vb_colour fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: ::: :::{.task} ::::{.task-header} Your turn :::: ::::{.task-container} * [ ] Change the x- and y-axis labels * [ ] Remove the legend * [ ] add a theme
::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(penguins, aes(x = species, y = body_mass_g, fill = species))+ geom_violin(alpha = 0.4) + geom_boxplot(width = 0.2) + scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Dark2", guide = "none")+ scale_x_discrete( # changing the label of x name = "Species", # changing the group labels of the 3 groups labels = c("Adelie penguin", "Chinstrap penguin", "Gentoo penguin")) + scale_y_continuous( # changing name of the y axis name = "Body mass (g)", # changing break labels breaks = c(seq(from = 3000, to = 6000, by = 500)) ) + theme_classic() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](12a-ggplot_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-30-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: :::
